title: The 0% Offer
intro: The best adverts in banking use the smallest number there is. Today you read the small print.

blocks.html:
An envelope arrives. Inside is an offer from the Brightline Card.

0% interest for 12 months!

Underneath, in much smaller letters:

3% transfer fee. 20% a year after the offer ends.

Here is the question for the board.

Zero percent of anything is nothing.

So is this offer free?

An analyst never answers that from the big print. She checks three things, and you are going to check all three:

1. What the fee costs on day one.
2. What happens in month 13.
3. What the minimum payment really pays off.

blocks.prompt:
Start with the fee. Marta owes £500 on an old card, and she wants to move it to the Brightline Card.

The transfer fee is 3% of the amount she moves.
blocks.hint: Find 1% first — divide by 100. Then three lots of that.

parts.label: 1% of £500 (£)
parts._working: 1% means one hundredth: 500 ÷ 100 = £5. Her 1% gear from w1s1, used exactly as taught.

blocks.prompt:
Now the part the advert does not mention.

The fee is not a bill that arrives separately. It is added straight onto what she owes.

So on day one, before she has paid a single penny of it off, her debt is bigger than it was.
blocks.hint: Add the fee to the £500 she moved. For the second one, find 1% of £1000 and take three of them.

parts.label: What Marta owes on day one, fee included (£)
parts._working: £500 moved plus the £15 fee = £515. She has borrowed nothing extra and bought nothing — the debt grew by £15 simply for accepting a 0% offer.

parts.label: If she had moved £1000 instead, the fee would be (£)
parts._working: 1% of £1000 = £10, so 3% = 3 × £10 = £30. The fee is a percentage, so it grows with the balance — the bigger the debt, the bigger the charge for moving it.

blocks.button: So why does the card company do this? ✨
blocks.html:
Nobody at Brightline is being kind.

Look at what they get.

They collect £15 on day one. That is their revenue, before the offer has even started.

And they have bought something far more valuable than £15.

They have bought Marta.

You have seen this before. Riverbend Books lost money on purpose to buy customers. Brightline is doing the same thing — giving away 12 months of interest to win someone who will probably still be there in month 13.

Because here is what the card company knows, and the advert does not say:

most people do not clear the balance in 12 months.

The offer is not a gift. It is a bet. And the house is betting on month 13.

blocks.prompt:
Month 13. The offer has ended.

Marta has been paying a little each month, and she still owes £400.

Now the real rate switches on — the one in the small print.
blocks.hint: The rate is in the small print at the top of the session. For the interest: find 10% of £400 first, then double it.

parts.label: The rate that switches on, from the small print (%)
parts._working: 20% a year, as printed. Both 20 and 0.2 are accepted because the engine reads a typed "20%" as 0.2 — without the decimal twin, a correct answer written with a percent sign would be marked wrong.

parts.label: Interest charged on the £400 in the first year after the offer (£)
parts._working: 10% of £400 = £40, so 20% = 2 × £40 = £80. (A real card adds its interest monthly rather than once a year, which makes it very slightly worse again — but the idea is the same and the monthly sum is not this unit's job.)

blocks.html:
Before the last check, you need to know the order things happen in. It is the whole trick.

Every month the card does two things, and always in this order.

First it adds the interest to what she owes.

Then it takes her payment off.

That order is not an accident.

It means her payment does not go to her debt first. It has to get past the interest before any of it counts.

Think of it as climbing a down escalator.

She is climbing. The escalator is pulling her back.

If she climbs faster than it pulls, she gets there — slowly.

If she climbs at the same speed, she stays exactly where she is, paying every month, for ever.

This is the snowball from last meeting. Same maths. It is just rolling the other way, and she is underneath it.

blocks.prompt:
Boss question. The last question assumed Marta paid nothing at all. That is not fair on her — she is paying. She pays the minimum payment of £10 every month.

So in one year she hands over £120 of her own money.

And the card charges her £80 of interest over that same year.

Here is the year, laid out.
The year after the offer ends£
Owed at the start of the year400
Interest added during the year80
Payments she made during the year120
Owed at the end of the year?
blocks.hint: Start with the £400. Add the interest on. Then take her payments off. Do it in that order, one step at a time.

parts.label: Owed at the end of the year (£)
So how much did the debt actually go down over the whole year? (£)
parts._working: 400 − 360 = £40. A year of paying, and the debt is only £40 smaller.

parts.label: She paid £120. Only part of it cleared the debt. How much went to the card company instead? (£)
parts._working: 120 − 40 = £80 — which is exactly the interest. Two thirds of every payment she made went to Brightline and never touched what she owed. This is w3s2's snowball, running against her: the interest is charged first, and her payment has to climb over it before any of it counts.

blocks.prompt:
★ The analyst's verdict. And the honest answer is not yes or no — it depends who is asking.

Two people get the same envelope. Both owe £500, so both would owe £515 after the fee.

Priya can afford £50 a month.
Dan can afford £10 a month.
blocks.hint: Work out what each of them actually pays over the 12 months of the offer. Then compare that with the £515 they owe.

parts.label: Paying £50 a month, what Priya pays over the 12 months of the offer (£)
parts._working: 12 × £50 = £600, which is more than the £515 she owes — so she clears it inside the offer and never pays a penny of interest. Her total cost is just the £15 fee.

parts.label: Paying £10 a month, what Dan still owes at the end of month 12 (£)
parts._working: 12 × £10 = £120 paid. £515 − £120 = £395 still owed when the offer ends — and on that, 20% a year switches on. His "0%" offer turns into a 20% debt of £395.

parts.label: So who should take this offer — Priya or Dan?
parts._working: Priya. Over the 12 months of the offer she pays 12 x £50 = £600, which is more than the £515 she owes, so she clears it inside the 0% window and the offer is genuinely good for her: she pays the £15 fee and nothing else. Dan pays 12 x £10 = £120 against £515, so he still owes £395 when month 13 arrives and the 20% switches on — the offer costs him the fee AND a year of lost time. Marked as TEXT, not a number: the natural answer to a 'who' question is a name, and the earlier numeric-only version would have shown 'Not yet - try again' to a child who typed priya. Accept list covers the name, common misspellings (never grade spelling for Grace), and the payment figure for anyone who answers the way the previous phrasing invited.

blocks.html:
📈 Field assignment, analyst — and this one is real:

This week, find an advert offering 0% or interest free. A card, a sofa, a phone, a car. They are everywhere once you start looking.

Find the small print. It is always there, and it is always smaller.

Then report to the board at dinner:

1. What did the advert want you to feel?
2. What is the fee, in real pounds, on £500?
3. What rate switches on at the end, and when exactly does it start?
4. Your verdict: who is this offer good for, and who is it a trap for?

Then the question to put to Dad: the card company knows most people will not clear the balance in time. Should they be allowed to call it 0%?

done.title: UNIT 3 COMPLETE 🍋✓
done.html:
The Bank is closed. Interest as rent on money — earned when you lend it, paid when you borrow it. Compounding, and the snowball that works for a saver and against a borrower. And now the hardest and most useful thing in the whole unit: reading the small print like an analyst, and finding the cost hidden inside the word free.

You worked out that a 0% offer costs £15 on day one, that two thirds of a minimum payment can vanish into interest, and that the same offer is a bargain for one person and a trap for another. Most adults sign these without doing any of that.

Next: Unit 4 — The Trading Floor. Shares, prices, and what a company is actually worth. Coming soon.
